steps.title: Express human calmodulin
steps.instruction: Transform BL21‑DE3 E. coli (or another suitable strain) with the pET‑14b vector containing the human CaM gene. Inoculate 1 L LB broth with 100 µg/mL ampicillin and grow at 37 °C from a glycerol stock until OD₆₀₀ reaches 0.8–1. Add 0.4 mM IPTG to induce expression and continue incubation for 4–6 h at 37 °C or overnight at 20 °C.

steps.title: Harvest and wash cells
steps.instruction: Centrifuge the culture at 9,000 × g for 9 min at 4 °C. Discard supernatant and wash the pellet twice with 50 mL fresh lysis buffer. Resuspend the final pellet in 30 mL lysis buffer and aliquot into 10 mL portions; store aliquots at –20 °C.

steps.title: Lyse cells and heat‑treat extract
steps.instruction: Thaw one 10 mL aliquot on ice. Sonicate three cycles of 10 s at 50 kHz, keeping the tube on ice. Perform three freeze–thaw cycles alternating between a dry‑ice/ethanol bath and a 37 °C water bath. Centrifuge the lysate at 14,000 × g for 15 min (microcentrifuge). Transfer the supernatant and heat it at 95 °C for 5 min, then centrifuge again at 14,000 × g for 15 min. This exploits CaM’s thermal stability.

steps.title: Phenyl‑Sepharose chromatography
steps.instruction: Add CaCl₂ to the clarified supernatant to a final concentration of 5 mM. Load the sample at room temperature onto a 5 mL Phenyl‑Sepharose column pre‑equilibrated with CQ buffer (gravity flow or peristaltic pump). Wash sequentially with 20 column volumes of CW buffer then 10 column volumes of CHSW buffer. Elute CaM with 20 column volumes of CE buffer, collecting 500 µL fractions.

steps.title: Analyze fractions by SDS‑PAGE
steps.instruction: Mix 20 µL of each elution fraction with 5 µL 5× loading buffer. Load onto a 15 % acrylamide gel and run in 1× running buffer at 120–150 V for 90 min. Stain the gel with Coomassie Brilliant Blue for 10 min, then destain 15 min with fast destaining solution followed by 30 min with regular destaining solution.

steps.title: Concentrate, dialyze and store CaM
steps.instruction: Concentrate pooled CaM fractions to ≥1 mg/mL using an Amicon Ultra‑15 mL 3 kDa centrifugal filter. Dialyze the concentrate against MilliQ water. Aliquot 1 mL portions, store at –20 °C (1 mg/mL) or lyophilize in 1 mL aliquots.

steps.title: Determine CaM concentration
steps.instruction: Measure absorbance at 276 nm (ε₂₇₆ = 3 030 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹) or perform a Bradford assay using unlabeled CaM as a standard.

steps.title: Prepare CaM for dansylation
steps.instruction: Dilute purified CaM in Dansylation buffer (D buffer) to 1 mg/mL.

steps.title: Prepare dansyl chloride solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve dansyl chloride in acetone to 2.17 mg/mL. Store the solution in the dark at 4 °C or –20 °C; it remains stable for months.

steps.title: Dansylate calmodulin
steps.instruction: Add 12.5 µL of the 2.17 mg/mL dansyl chloride solution to 1 mL of the 1 mg/mL CaM solution (final dansyl chloride ≈100 µM). Incubate at room temperature in the dark for 2 h, vortexing gently every 20 min.

steps.title: Separate D‑CaM from excess reagent
steps.instruction: Equilibrate ~250 mg dry Sephadex G‑25 resin with distilled water. Pack a disposable column with ~1 mL resin. Load the reaction mixture, then collect fractions of 50–100 µL. The first (“excluded”) fractions contain the dansyl‑labeled CaM (D‑CaM).

steps.title: Analyze D‑CaM fractions
steps.instruction: Perform dot‑blot on nitrocellulose and stain with Ponceau Red. Run 15 % SDS‑PAGE gels of the fractions. Record emission spectra (excitation 340 nm, emission 400–660 nm) at 25 °C; a peak near 500 nm indicates successful labeling.

steps.title: Store dansyl‑CaM
steps.instruction: Concentrate D‑CaM if needed, adjust to 0.5–5 µM, and store aliquots in the dark at –20 °C or lyophilize. The conjugate remains stable for several months at –20 °C.

steps.title: Determine D‑CaM concentration
steps.instruction: Use a Bradford assay with unlabeled CaM as standard, or measure UV absorbance at 320 nm (ε₃₂₀ = 3 400 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹). Determine the dansyl moiety concentration by spectroscopy and calculate the average number of labeled residues per CaM molecule.

steps.title: Resuspend peptides
steps.instruction:
Dissolve peptides in sterile distilled water (suitable for <5‑residue peptides). For each peptide, calculate net charge: –1 per Asp, Glu, C‑terminal COOH; +1 per Arg, Lys, His, N‑terminal NH₂. 
• Positive net charge: try water; if insoluble, add 10–30 % acetic acid; if still insoluble, add <50 µL TFA then dilute to desired concentration. 
• Negative net charge: try water; if insoluble, add <50 µL NH₄OH then dilute. 
• Net zero charge: add organic solvent—acetonitrile, methanol, or isopropanol; for highly hydrophobic peptides add 30–50 µL 100 % DMSO (or DMF if cysteine present). Add dropwise to a stirring aqueous buffer (e.g., PBS) until the target concentration is reached. If turbidity appears, the solubility limit is reached; sonication can aid dissolution. For aggregating peptides, pre‑treat with 6 M guanidine·HCl or 8 M urea before dilution.

steps.title: Apo‑CaM peptide titration
steps.instruction:
Dilute each peptide stock in Fluorescence buffer (F buffer) to 20 µM. Prepare 100 µL assay mixtures according to Table 1 (final D‑CaM 1 µM, peptide concentrations 0–8 µM, balance with Fluorescence buffer). Table 1 composition:

| Peptide µM | D‑CaM µL | Peptide µL | F buffer µL |
|-----------|----------|------------|------------|
| 0         | 5        | 0          | 95         |
| 0.1       | 5        | 0.5        | 94.5       |
| 0.2       | 5        | 1          | 94         |
| 0.5       | 5        | 2.5        | 92.5       |
| 1         | 5        | 5          | 90         |
| 1.5       | 5        | 7.5        | 87.5       |
| 2         | 5        | 10         | 85         |
| 4         | 5        | 20         | 75         |
| 8         | 5        | 40         | 55         |
| 16        | 5        | 80         | 15         |

Centrifuge each sample at 185 494 × g (radius 98 mm) for 10 min, transfer supernatant to fresh 500 µL tubes, avoiding bubbles. Record emission spectra on a fluorimeter (excitation 340 nm, emission 400–660 nm) at 25 °C; correct for buffer background. The D‑CaM spectrum should show a peak near 500 nm. Record fluorescence values for each peptide concentration.

steps.title: Calcium titration of apo‑CaM complexes
steps.instruction:
Using the peptide‑saturated sample (100 µL) from the previous step, add 1 µL of Calcium buffer (Ca buffer, 10 mM CaCl₂, 120 mM KCl, 50 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 5 mM NaCl, 5 mM EGTA) sequentially. After each 1 µL addition, mix thoroughly and record emission spectra 20–30 s later (same settings as above). Perform additions until the fluorescence no longer changes (saturation). Calculate free Ca²⁺ concentrations using the Ca‑EGTA Calculator v1.3 (Table 2):

| Ca buffer µL | Total µL | [Ca²⁺] total (mM) | [Ca²⁺] free (µM) |
|--------------|----------|-------------------|------------------|
| 0            | 100      | 0                 | 0                |
| 1            | 101      | 0.1               | 0.0030           |
| 2            | 102      | 0.2               | 0.0079           |
| 3            | 103      | 0.3               | 0.177            |
| 4            | 104      | 0.4               | 0.471            |
| 5            | 105      | 0.5               | 2.45             |
| 6            | 106      | 0.6               | 10.01            |
| 7            | 107      | 0.7               | 20               |
| 8            | 108      | 0.8               | 30               |
| 9            | 109      | 0.9               | 40               |
|10            | 110      | 1.0               | 50               |

All measurements are at pH 7.4 and 25 °C; EGTA buffering is pH‑dependent.

steps.title: Holo‑CaM peptide titration
steps.instruction:
First saturate CaM with 1 mM free CaCl₂ (using Ca buffer). Prepare 100 µL assay mixtures according to Table 3 (final D‑CaM 1 µM, peptide concentrations 0–8 µM, 10 µL Ca buffer added to each). Table 3 composition:

| Peptide µM | Peptide µL | F buffer µL | Ca buffer µL | Total µL |
|-----------|-----------|------------|------------|----------|
| 0         | 0         | 90         | 10         | 100      |
| 0.2       | 1         | 89         | 10         | 100      |
| 0.5       | 2.5       | 87.5       | 10         | 100      |
| 1         | 5         | 85         | 10         | 100      |
| 2         | 10        | 80         | 10         | 100      |
| 4         | 20        | 70         | 10         | 100      |
| 8         | 40        | 50         | 10         | 100      |
| 16        | 80        | 10         | 10         | 100      |

Centrifuge each sample at 185 494 × g for 10 min, transfer supernatant to fresh tubes, avoid bubbles. Record emission spectra (excitation 340 nm, emission 400–660 nm) at 25 °C with the same buffer corrections. Capture fluorescence values for each peptide concentration.

description: Validation of protocol This methodology, initially validated by Kincaid and Vaughan in 1986 [17], has exhibited consistent efficacy in discerning conformational changes resulting from interactions with Ca 2+ , peptides, or proteins. Subsequent studies Yuan by and Graves in 1989 [18] investigated the interaction of CaM with the γ subunit of phosphorylase kinase, while Munier et al. in 1991 [19] characterized the catalytic and calmodulin-binding domains of Bordetella pertussis adenylate cyclase (refer to Figures 3 and 4). Filoteo et al. [20] delved into the binding between the lipid-binding region (G region) of the erythrocyte Ca 2+ pump and CaM (see Figures 4 and 5). In 2013, Alaimo et al. [14] explored the interaction of CaM with different components of the Kv7.2 channel (refer to Figures 5, 6, and 7). Zhang et al. [21] identified two distinct CaM binding sites in the angiotensin II (AT1A) receptor (refer to Figures 4 and 6). Alcalde et al. [22] demonstrated that non-myristoylated peptides derived from the CaM binding site of Grb7 exhibit higher efficiency in binding dansyl-CaM in the presence of Ca 2+ compared to its absence (see Supplementary Figure 2). More recently, Nuñez et al. [23] showcased that the oxidation of peptides derived from the S2S3 linker of Kv7 channels inhibits their binding to CaM (refer to Figure 3), and numerous other studies contribute to the comprehensive utility of this method.
